passage: For the third night in a row, Hana asked the same question at bedtime in their Oslo flat. 'Pappa, where is Mormor now?' Anders gave the same answer: 'Mormor died. Her body stopped working, and she can't come back. We remember her.' Hana nodded. In the afternoons she lined up her stuffed animals, laid the rabbit in a shoebox and made the bear sing a slow song. Every Sunday at four, when Mormor used to arrive with cinnamon buns, Hana still ran to the window. 'Maybe she's late,' she said once. Anders didn't correct her sharply. He just sat with her by the glass until she turned away on her own.

qa.q: What did Mormor use to bring on Sundays at four?
qa.a: Mormor used to arrive with cinnamon buns.

qa.q: Why does Hana keep asking the same question every night?
qa.a: Hana is still confused and missing Mormor; repeating the question helps her slowly make the loss real, as each honest answer lets a little more sink in.

qa.q: What is Anders doing that helps Hana at this stage?
qa.a: He gives the same short, honest answer each time and sits with her at the window instead of scolding or distracting her.

qa.q: What might it be like for Anders to answer the same question night after night?
qa.a: It is probably painful, since the loss may be his too, yet he stays patient because he sees Hana needs it 🤍.

grounding: A grieving girl repeats the same question, acts out a funeral with toys and still watches for her grandmother, slowly making the loss real.

passage: In the Class 3 play corner, Siddharth had built a small stretcher from rulers and laid a toy soldier on it. He walked it slowly across the mat while two friends hummed. 'This is Nana's funeral,' he told Manoj sir, quite matter-of-fact. At lunch he asked again, 'Sir, where do people go when they die? Where did Nana go?' He had asked the same thing on Monday and Wednesday. And every day at the gate, he looked for Nana's blue scooter before remembering. Manoj sir crouched down each time. 'People believe different things about where we go. What does your family say?' Siddharth thought. 'Ma says he's in our hearts.' 'Then that's a good place to keep him.'

qa.q: What did Siddharth look for every day at the gate?
qa.a: He looked for Nana's blue scooter.

qa.q: What does Siddharth acting out Nana's funeral suggest he is doing inside?
qa.a: He seems sad and to be grieving Nana, replaying the funeral in play so that the loss slowly becomes real to him.

qa.q: Why is Manoj sir's answer about where people go a wise one?
qa.a: He is honest that beliefs differ and lets Siddharth bring his family's words, which respects the home's beliefs and still answers patiently.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's friends experience humming at the play funeral?
qa.a: They may treat it as an ordinary game or feel a little unsure, but joining in helps Siddharth feel less alone.

grounding: At school a grieving boy acts out his grandfather's funeral, repeats questions about where he went and still looks for him at the gate.

passage:
Damini, beta, you asked why I keep Baba's old umbrella by the door. Let me tell you.
When my father died, I was nine. For weeks I asked Aai the same things, every night. Where is Baba? Can he see us? When is he coming back? Aai answered every time, quietly: "He died. His body stopped working. He can't come back."
I played funerals with my dolls. I laid them on a cloth and put marigolds on them. My aunts were shocked. Aai let me.
And every evening at seven, I'd look at the door, waiting for his umbrella to come through it.
It took months. Asking again and again was how I, Parul, slowly believed it.

qa.q: How old was Parul when her father died?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was young Parul feeling as she waited at the door each evening?
qa.a: She felt a longing and hope that her Baba might walk in, as the loss was not yet real to her.

qa.q: In the story, what choice did Aai make that helped Parul?
qa.a: Aai answered the same questions honestly and patiently every night and let her play funerals, instead of stopping her.

qa.q: How might Aai have felt answering the same question every night?
qa.a: Aai was probably grieving too and tired, but chose patience because Parul needed the answers again.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a grieving child, she asked the same questions, played funerals and waited at the door until the loss became real.

passage:
Exam week, a power cut, and a house still full of relatives: it was the worst time for questions, but Sonali kept asking them.
"Masi, where did Mamma go? Is she in the sky? Can she hear me?"
Jahnavi Masi was lighting a candle so Sonali could finish her maths. "She died, Sonu. Her body stopped. She can't come back, but we can remember her."
"But where is she?"
The same question, for the fourth time that evening. Jahnavi answered again.
Later, Sonali lined up her teddies and covered one with a dupatta. "This is the funeral," she whispered. Then she looked at the door, as if someone might walk in.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi Masi lighting?
qa.a: A candle, so Sonali could finish her maths.

qa.q: What does Sonali looking at the door suggest?
qa.a: She still hopes and longs for her Mamma to walk in, as the loss is not fully real to her yet.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi Masi doing well, even in a hard week?
qa.a: Answering the same question honestly and patiently each time, which helps Sonali slowly make the loss real.

qa.q: What might the teddy funeral mean for Sonali?
qa.a: Playing it out may be how she tries to understand what happened to her Mamma, a normal part of grieving.

grounding: Shows a grieving child asking the same questions, acting out a funeral with toys and looking for her mother at the door.

passage:
Every evening in their Nagpur flat, Vikas asked his mother the same question. "Aai, where did Aaji go?"
Irawati would stop cooking and answer. "Aaji died, Vikas. Her body stopped working. She isn't anywhere we can visit."
"But where?"
In the day he played with his cars, lining them up like the cars outside the crematorium. He made the cars go slowly. He made them stop. Then he started again.
On Sunday, when the doorbell rang, he ran to it shouting, "Aaji!" It was the milkman. Vikas stood very still.
Irawati knelt and held him. "You were hoping it was Aaji." He nodded into her shoulder.

qa.q: Who was at the door on Sunday?
qa.a: The milkman.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he stood very still at the door?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and sad, having hoped Aaji had come back.

qa.q: What small thing did Irawati do that helped at this stage?
qa.a: She knelt, held him and named his hope, rather than dismissing it or distracting him.

qa.q: What is it like for Irawati to answer the same question every evening?
qa.a: She is likely grieving herself and tired, yet chooses to stop cooking and answer patiently each time.

grounding: Shows a grieving child asking the same question, replaying the funeral with toy cars and running to the door expecting his grandmother.

passage:
"Mumma, where did Nana go? Like, exactly?" Kunal asked, lining up his toy soldiers on the carpet.
"You asked that yesterday, remember?" Madhuri said gently, folding clothes. "Nana died. His body stopped working, and he won't come back."
"But where is he now?"
"Different people believe different things. Nana used to say he'd be up with the stars."
Kunal laid one soldier on a hanky and covered it. "This is Nana. Everyone has to walk slowly and put flowers."
"Okay," Madhuri said, and sat down beside him.
"When the bell rings at seven, can we check? He always came at seven with jalebi."
Madhuri swallowed. "The bell might ring, beta. It won't be Nana. I wish it could be."
Kunal was quiet, then asked, "Can I ask again tomorrow?"
"You can ask every day."

qa.q: What did Kunal use to cover the soldier?
qa.a: He covered it with a hanky.

qa.q: Why might Kunal keep asking where Nana went?
qa.a: He is still confused and sad, and asking again and again is how he slowly makes the loss feel real.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's approach get right?
qa.a: She answers honestly and briefly, joins his play and lets him ask every day instead of changing the subject.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri when Kunal mentions the seven o'clock bell?
qa.a: She swallows hard, feeling her own grief too, while still answering him gently and truthfully.

grounding: Shows a grieving child repeating questions, acting out a funeral in play and expecting the grandparent to arrive at the usual time.
